articles.title: Sudan war: $22 million education boost to help 200,000 children
articles.summary: For millions of children in Sudan, the classroom remains out of reach as the country’s civil war continues to disrupt their education. To help tackle this huge problem, the UN global education fund on Monday announced a $22 million initiative to help 200,000 youngsters return to learning.
articles.content:
The three Sudanese states receiving support are West Darfur, South Kordofan and Gedaref, where the aim is to restore “safe, quality and inclusive education”, amid the world’s largest humanitarian and displacement crisis.

Tweet URL

Maysa Jalbout, Director of Education Cannot Wait, insisted that education remains one of the most powerful tools in the humanitarian toolbox to protect millions of children and support recovery.

“This investment is about much more than reopening classrooms. It is about supporting children to regain a sense of safety and normalcy while strengthening education systems that can continue serving communities through crisis and into recovery.”

A humanitarian emergency

Since conflict erupted in April 2023 between the country’s rival militaries, 14 million people have been forced to flee their homes and 33.7 million people now require humanitarian assistance.

Announcing the multi-year investment initiative, Education Cannot Wait said that at least eight million children – nearly half of Sudan’s 17 million school-age children – are still out of school.

“Across the country, large numbers of schools remain non-operational, while millions of children have endured prolonged disruptions to their education, with some missing nearly 500 days of learning,” the organization stressed.

The three-year programme will reach those left furthest behind in the country – including internally displaced children, refugees and vulnerable host communities, with at least 60 per cent girls and 10 per cent children with disabilities.

The initiative will establish safe learning environments, provide mental health and psychosocial support, strengthen teacher capacity, improve access to learning materials and address barriers facing girls and children with disabilities.

Implementation will be led by Save the Children, in partnership with Plan International, Lakarmissionen International (LM International), and local partners Alsalam Organisation for Relief and Development (AORD) and Sadagaat.

In its mid-year update on Sudan, the UN Children’s Fund, UNICEF, said that 81 per cent of schools in Darfur remain closed, 70 per cent of children there are not attending school, and 5.8 per cent of schools are being used as shelters. It also says schools have come under direct attack this year.

Worldwide needs

According to Education Cannot Wait, 258 million school-aged children and teens in crisis are affected by disrupted learning worldwide. Of these, 93 million are out of school altogether.

A recent report from the UN’s global education fund found that nearly 80 per cent of children unable to go to school because of crises or conflict live in just 20 countries.

Often it is the most marginalized groups that suffer the most exclusion, especially girls, displaced youngsters and children with disabilities.

The Sudan announcement comes as Education Cannot Wait launches the global campaign - Hope Starts Here - to mobilize $600 million to reach 10 million children whose learning continues to be impacted by the world’s most severe crises.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England
articles.summary: Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands and West Yorkshire as well as £6bn for London.
articles.content:
The 22-year-old spent the final months of her pregnancy and the first weeks of her son's life living in a hotel.

She says she has no idea how long she will be expected to stay there but was told it would only be temporary.

"I'm just scared when he gets older, when he starts crawling around, I can't even allow him to crawl in such a place like that because it's so dirty," she says.

While pregnant, Natasha says her room became infested with ants, which she repeatedly reported before eventually being moved into another room.

But her problems didn't end there.

While Natasha has her own bathroom, she shares a kitchen with around 60 other residents. She says the hotel is home to a mix of people, not just mothers and babies, and that she does not always feel safe using the shared space with Zayd.

Natasha describes living there as feeling "like a prison". She says visitors are not allowed, meaning friends and family can not come to help her with her five-week-old boy.

"I just want somewhere peaceful for him and calm. Somewhere nice where I can bring him up," she says.

She is one of the 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

London will see the largest share of funding, although no figure has been given for how many homes will be built in the capital.

Ministers said Monday's allocation was the first stage of the 10-year programme and more than £16bn remains to be allocated outside London.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested some of the new homes will be built by councils, saying she and the prime minister were "doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Burnham had previously promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period", and the government said millions extra would be given to councils to support their housebuilding plans and help with expertise.

But the announcement stops short of clarifying how the funding will be split between council homes and those provided by housing associations.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant government funding initiative to build over 70,000 social and affordable homes across England, addressing a critical housing shortage affecting over a million households. This has broad societal impact by aiming to improve living conditions and provide stable housing for vulnerable populations, including families currently living in inadequate conditions. The story provides sufficient context about the scale, funding allocation, and intended beneficiaries, making it a substantial positive development in social welfare and housing rights.

**What happened** – The government announced funding to build more than 70,000 new social and affordable homes across England. This includes money given to areas like Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, and £6 billion allocated for London. This is part of a 10-year plan to improve housing.

**Impact** – This funding aims to help families living in unsafe or overcrowded places find better, more secure homes. For example, Natasha, who spent months in a hotel with poor conditions, represents the many people who will benefit. The plan also supports councils to build more homes, which could increase the number of affordable housing options.

**What's next step** – More than £16 billion is still to be allocated outside London to continue building new homes. The government will work with councils and housing groups to decide how to use this money and make sure the homes meet people’s needs.

**One-sentence takeaway** – England’s government is investing in thousands of new social homes to provide safer, affordable places for families currently living in difficult conditions.

articles.title: Poisoned waters: Indigenous communities fight to protect Thailand’s Kok River
articles.summary: "For Indigenous communities in northern Thailand, protecting the Kok River is inseparable from protecting their lands, livelihoods, and cultural heritage."
articles.content:
This edited article by Sheikh Mehzabin Chitra was published by Prachatai, an independent news site in Thailand. An edited version has been republished by Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

Hundreds of villagers, Indigenous leaders, environmental defenders, monks, and civil society activists completed a six-day Peace Walk in July along northern Thailand’s Kok River to demand urgent action against worsening water contamination. Their message was clear: The river that has sustained communities for generations is becoming increasingly unsafe, and stronger action is needed to stop transboundary pollution before irreversible damage is done.

The Kok River originates in Myanmar’s Shan State, flows through Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai provinces, and eventually joins the Mekong River. For communities living along its banks, the river provides drinking water, irrigation, fisheries, transportation, and cultural identity. Today, however, many residents fear that these lifelines are under threat from heavy metal contamination linked to mining operations upstream in Myanmar.

The Peace Walk has become one of the largest recent demonstrations calling for accountability over pollution affecting the Kok, Sai, Ruak, and Mekong rivers. Participants urged the Thai government to strengthen cross-border cooperation, investigate the source of contamination, and protect communities whose livelihoods depend on healthy river ecosystems.

A growing transboundary pollution crisis

Concerns over the Kok River have intensified following reports of elevated concentrations of heavy metals, including arsenic, in rivers flowing from Myanmar into northern Thailand. Environmental groups and local communities have linked the contamination to expanding rare earth and mineral mining operations in Myanmar, reportedly financed by Chinese investors.

The issue extends beyond environmental degradation. Farmers rely on river water to irrigate crops, while fishing communities depend on healthy aquatic ecosystems for food and income. Public health authorities have also advised caution regarding the consumption of aquatic animals from contaminated rivers because of heavy metal exposure.

Civil society organizations warn that contamination now affects not only the Kok River but also the Sai, Ruak, Salween, and Mekong rivers. According to the NGO Coordinating Committee on Development (NGO-COD), turbidity along sections of the Thai-Myanmar border has increased dramatically, while arsenic and lead contamination have exceeded recommended safety levels in several communities.

Because these rivers cross national boundaries, downstream communities often bear the environmental consequences of activities occurring beyond Thailand’s jurisdiction. Environmental advocates argue that stronger regional cooperation between Thailand, Myanmar, and China is necessary to investigate pollution sources, improve monitoring, and prevent further contamination.

Communities demand accountability

Public concern has grown alongside frustration over the perceived lack of effective action.

Members of the People's Network to Protect the Kok, Sai, Ruak, and Mekong Rivers marched toward the Chinese Consulate-General in Chiang Mai on July 6th to deliver a petition urging China to regulate Chinese companies operating mines in Myanmar. Protesters argued that mining activities have contributed to heavy metal contamination affecting millions of people living downstream.

Before the demonstrators reached the Consulate-General, however, they faced a police blockade. A confrontation occurred when police tried to seize a protest banner carried by one of the demonstrators, leaving two protesters injured. One has a broken arm, and another has a dislocated shoulder. The protesters filed a police complaint alleging excessive use of force, while the police maintained that officers acted in accordance with legal procedure. One of the injured protesters, Wisarut Srichan, is also considering filing lawsuits against the police.

Two days later, civil society organizations gathered outside the Chinese Embassy in Bangkok to demand action regarding the water contamination and condemn the police response in Chiang Mai. They called for an independent investigation into the use of force against protesters and urged authorities to identify investment networks and business operations responsible for environmental harm and human rights violations.

Environmental defenders under pressure

Protesters in Chiang Mai said they did not expect a confrontation, as the march was small and they had already informed the police beforehand. But physical violence is not the only threat faced by environmental activists in Thailand.

Human rights organizations have documented the increasing use of Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPPs) against community leaders, journalists, researchers, and activists who speak out about the environmental impacts of development projects. Such lawsuits often impose significant financial and psychological burdens even when the charges are eventually dismissed.

One widely cited case involved environmental defender Sumeth Rainpongnam, who faced a 50-million-baht (USD 1.5 million) lawsuit while advocating for community environmental rights. Rights organizations argue that these cases discourage public participation and make it more difficult for affected communities to raise environmental concerns.

Indigenous communities protecting rivers

For Indigenous communities in northern Thailand, protecting the Kok River is inseparable from protecting their lands, livelihoods, and cultural heritage.

Karen and other Indigenous communities have long resisted projects they believe threaten forests and river systems. In Omkoi District, Karen villagers challenged a proposed coal mining project, arguing that environmental impact assessments failed to adequately consider Indigenous knowledge and local ecosystems. Communities have also opposed the Yuam–Salween Water Diversion Project, citing concerns over its potential impacts on forests, fisheries, and water resources while questioning whether affected communities were meaningfully consulted during the approval process.

These campaigns reflect a broader understanding of environmental stewardship. For many Indigenous peoples, rivers are living ecosystems that sustain culture, food systems, and future generations, not simply natural resources to be exploited.

Participants in the Kok River Peace Walk emphasized that communities who have lived alongside these rivers for generations possess valuable ecological knowledge that should guide conservation efforts. They called for stronger recognition of Indigenous land rights, meaningful community participation in environmental decision-making, transparent environmental monitoring, and greater protection for environmental defenders.

As northern Thailand continues to confront the impacts of transboundary pollution, many residents argue that protecting the Kok River requires more than emergency responses. It demands sustained regional cooperation, corporate accountability, and greater recognition of Indigenous communities whose stewardship has long helped safeguard the region's rivers.

For those who completed the Peace Walk, protecting the Kok River is ultimately about more than preserving a waterway. It is about defending public health, cultural survival, and the rights of future generations to inherit rivers that remain safe, living, and free from contamination.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights Indigenous communities and environmental defenders actively mobilizing to protect the Kok River from transboundary pollution, emphasizing their cultural and livelihood rights. It reports a significant grassroots movement demanding government and corporate accountability, cross-border cooperation, and recognition of Indigenous stewardship, which has broad societal and environmental implications. The story focuses on a single, meaningful issue with detailed context about environmental contamination, community activism, and human rights challenges, making it an inspiring example of community resilience and advocacy for environmental justice.
articles.personality_title: Communities unite to protect Thailand’s Kok River from pollution
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Kok River flows through northern Thailand and Myanmar, supporting local communities with water for drinking, farming, fishing, and cultural traditions. Recently, pollution from mining in Myanmar has threatened the river’s health.

**What happened** – In July 2026, hundreds of villagers, Indigenous leaders, monks, and activists completed a six-day Peace Walk along the Kok River. They called for urgent action to stop heavy metal contamination, especially arsenic, linked to mining upstream. Protesters also marched to Chinese diplomatic offices, urging regulation of Chinese companies involved in mining. Some protesters faced police violence during demonstrations.

**Impact** – This movement is one of the largest efforts demanding cleaner rivers and accountability for pollution affecting millions downstream. The pollution harms farming, fishing, and public health. Indigenous communities emphasize that protecting the river is key to preserving their culture and land. The protests highlight the need for better cooperation between Thailand, Myanmar, and China to monitor and stop contamination.

**What's next step** – Activists want governments to investigate pollution sources, strengthen cross-border cooperation, and respect Indigenous land rights. They also seek protection for environmental defenders facing lawsuits and pressure. The Peace Walk has raised awareness that lasting solutions require regional teamwork and community involvement.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Indigenous and local communities are leading a powerful movement to protect the Kok River’s water and culture from harmful pollution across borders.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les communautés unies pour protéger la rivière Kok en Thaïlande de la pollution
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La rivière Kok traverse le nord de la Thaïlande et le Myanmar, fournissant de l’eau potable, de l’eau pour l’agriculture, la pêche et soutenant les traditions culturelles des communautés locales. Récemment, la pollution liée à l’exploitation minière au Myanmar menace la santé de la rivière.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En juillet 2026, des centaines de villageois, leaders autochtones, moines et militants ont réalisé une marche de paix de six jours le long de la rivière Kok. Ils ont demandé une action urgente pour arrêter la contamination aux métaux lourds, notamment l’arsenic, liée à l’exploitation minière en amont. Les manifestants ont aussi marché vers les bureaux diplomatiques chinois pour demander la régulation des entreprises chinoises impliquées dans l’exploitation minière. Certains manifestants ont subi des violences policières.

**Impact** – Ce mouvement est l’une des plus grandes mobilisations récentes exigeant des rivières plus propres et la responsabilité face à la pollution qui touche des millions de personnes en aval. La pollution nuit à l’agriculture, à la pêche et à la santé publique. Les communautés autochtones soulignent que protéger la rivière est essentiel pour préserver leur culture et leurs terres. Ces protestations montrent la nécessité d’une meilleure coopération entre la Thaïlande, le Myanmar et la Chine pour surveiller et stopper la contamination.

**Prochaine étape** – Les militants souhaitent que les gouvernements enquêtent sur les sources de pollution, renforcent la coopération transfrontalière et respectent les droits fonciers autochtones. Ils demandent aussi la protection des défenseurs de l’environnement face aux poursuites judiciaires et pressions. La marche de paix a sensibilisé au fait que des solutions durables demandent un travail d’équipe régional et la participation des communautés.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les communautés autochtones et locales mènent un mouvement fort pour protéger l’eau et la culture de la rivière Kok contre une pollution nuisible qui traverse les frontières.
articles.personality_title_es: Comunidades se unen para proteger el río Kok en Tailandia de la contaminación
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El río Kok atraviesa el norte de Tailandia y Myanmar, proporcionando agua para beber, agricultura, pesca y apoyando las tradiciones culturales de las comunidades locales. Recientemente, la contaminación proveniente de la minería en Myanmar ha puesto en riesgo la salud del río.

**Qué pasó** – En julio de 2026, cientos de aldeanos, líderes indígenas, monjes y activistas completaron una Caminata de Paz de seis días a lo largo del río Kok. Exigieron acciones urgentes para detener la contaminación por metales pesados, especialmente arsénico, vinculada a la minería aguas arriba. Los manifestantes también marcharon hacia oficinas diplomáticas chinas para pedir regulación de las empresas chinas involucradas en la minería. Algunos manifestantes enfrentaron violencia policial.

**Impacto** – Este movimiento es uno de los mayores esfuerzos recientes para exigir ríos más limpios y responsabilidad por la contaminación que afecta a millones río abajo. La contaminación daña la agricultura, la pesca y la salud pública. Las comunidades indígenas destacan que proteger el río es clave para preservar su cultura y tierras. Las protestas muestran la necesidad de mejor cooperación entre Tailandia, Myanmar y China para monitorear y detener la contaminación.

**Próximo paso** – Los activistas quieren que los gobiernos investiguen las fuentes de contaminación, fortalezcan la cooperación transfronteriza y respeten los derechos territoriales indígenas. También buscan protección para los defensores ambientales frente a demandas y presiones. La Caminata de Paz ha aumentado la conciencia de que se necesitan soluciones duraderas con trabajo regional y participación comunitaria.

**Resumen en una frase** – Comunidades indígenas y locales lideran un movimiento fuerte para proteger el agua y la cultura del río Kok de la contaminación dañina que cruza fronteras.

articles.title: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tips
articles.summary: Tips are central to US dining culture but some eateries think that they are unfair.
articles.content:
Wine waiter Caroline Kraetzer earns $40 (£30) an hour, double what most service staff in San Francisco are paid but then it costs a lot to eat at her restaurant.

At a set price of $140 (£100) per person, La Cigale is one of a small number of restaurants charging higher prices so it can pay high salaries - and it doesn't allow tips.

It tells customers: "What you see is what you pay. We do not accept tips, your kind words and return visits will suffice."

Kraetzer says it is good to no longer be "reliant on the generosity of strangers to pay the bills".

While waiting staff at other restaurants can make a lot of money from tips, she says "you're often there two hours before service, and again when you're closing after the guests have left, so you are making minimum wage during that time".
